extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing patent subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the two-step/Mayo-Alice framework (Step 2A marked-difference/product-of-nature analysis and Step 2B 'significantly more' inventive-concept analysis). Intended to direct claim-level examination and rejection drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics (product-of-nature analysis, Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nature-based product recited in a claim, determine whether the product has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. If it does, the claim does not recite a 'product of nature' exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible unless the claim recites another exception; if it does not, the claim is directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES) and the analysis proceeds to Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered when determining whether there is a marked difference include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (including functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic or physical). For single nature-based product claims, a showing of a markedly different characteristic is sufficient for eligibility (no Step 2B needed). If a 101 rejection is made, identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain why the product does not have markedly different characteristics (provide reasons referencing the naturally occurring counterpart). Examples: Chakrabarty (genetically modified bacterium with new degradative ability found markedly different); Myriad (isolated DNA identical to natural gene not markedly different; cDNA/exons-only sequence may be markedly different).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B - 'Significantly more' (inventive concept) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim determined to be directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element or combination of elements in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself (the search for an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the claim as a whole: individual elements viewed alone may not add significantly more, but their combination might. A claim directed to an exception must include additional features that apply the exception in a meaningful way and are not merely drafting to monopolize the exception. Every claim must be examined individually based on its particular elements and ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of limitations that may qualify as 'significantly more' (positive indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that may be enough to qualify as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exhaustive examples include: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; and other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment. (Citations: Diehr, Alice, Bilski, Mayo as discussed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that are not enough to qualify as 'significantly more' (negative indicators / anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claim limitations or additions that courts have found insufficient to transform a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations found not enough include: adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) with the judicial exception, or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; simply appending well-understood, routine and conventional activities previously known to the industry (specified at a high level of generality); adding insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea); and generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (field-of-use limitation). (Citations: Alice, Mayo, Flook, Benson, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claim elements individually and as ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether individual claim elements, or their ordered combination, supply the necessary 'something more' to transform an exception into an eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual elements that seem insignificant on their own may, when considered as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Conversely, an ordered combination that merely joins routine computer functions or conventional steps may still fail. Always analyze the claim as a whole and avoid automatically treating similar claims in an application as standing or falling together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure when a claim is directed to a plurality of judicial exceptions (e.g., a law of nature plus an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions. If the claim recites an element or combination that amounts to significantly more than that exception, consider whether those additional elements also amount to significantly more for the other claimed exception(s) to ensure no preemption. Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in the claim. If the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible and no further eligibility analysis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (efficiency for clearly eligible claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: For efficiency, use a streamlined eligibility analysis for claims that may or may not recite a judicial exception but clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception; full analysis not required where eligibility is self-evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations along with a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system), an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral, or products that merely include ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with a gold electrical contact or plastic chair with wood trim). If there is doubt whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for the judicial exception itself, perform the full analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection drafting and identification of the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, examiners must identify how the exception is recited in the claim and explain why the claim is considered to recite an exception or lacks markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should: identify the exception as it is recited (set forth or described) in the claim; explain why it is an exception; explain why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart when applicable; if the claim includes additional elements, identify those elements and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception. See MPEP 2103(VI) and 2106(III) for guidance on making the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete examination under all patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection is made, examiners must perform a complete examination of every claim under the other patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty), 103 (non-obviousness), 112 (specification/claims requirements including utility, inventorship and double patenting), and consider non-statutory double patenting as applicable. See MPEP 2103 et seq. and 2106(III).
